title: Contraction Control
intro: I'm becomes I am. Can't becomes cannot. Knowing when NOT to contract in formal writing is its own skill.

options: I am writing to apply for the position.
I'm writing to apply for the position.
I is writing to apply for the position.
A2.why: In a formal letter, write “I am” in full; “I'm” is for friends and chat.

options: We cannot attend the meeting.
We can't attend the meeting.
We not can attend the meeting.
A2.why: “Cannot” is one word in its full form; “can't” sounds too casual for formal writing.

options: It is important to arrive on time.
It's important to arrive on time.
Its important to arrive on time.
A2.why: Formal style keeps “it is” in full. And “its” without an apostrophe means “de ello”.

options: They do not agree with the proposal.
They don't agree with the proposal.
They not agree with the proposal.
A2.why: Formal writing uses “do not” in full; “don't” belongs in speech and casual messages.

options: She will not be attending the event.
She won't be attending the event.
She wont be attending the event.
A2.why: “Will not” is the full form of “won't”; “wont” with no apostrophe is a spelling mistake.

options: I would like to request more information.
I'd like to request more information.
I like to request more information.
A2.why: “I would like” is the polite, formal request; “I'd like” is the spoken version.

options: We are pleased to confirm your booking.
We're pleased to confirm your booking.
We pleased to confirm your booking.
A2.why: Business letters keep “we are” in full, and English never drops the verb “are”.

options: He has not replied to my email yet.
He hasn't replied to my email yet.
He have not replied to my email yet.
A2.why: “Has not” in full suits a formal email; “he have” is wrong because “he” takes “has”.

options: I have attached the report for your review.
I've attached the report for your review.
I has attached the report for your review.
A2.why: “I have attached” in full is standard in formal emails; “I has” breaks the verb.

options: The museum is not open on Mondays.
The museum isn't open on Mondays.
The museum not is open on Mondays.
A2.why: Formal notices write “is not” in full, and “not” goes after “is”, never before it.

options: I do not have a reservation for this evening.
I don't have a reservation for this evening.
I not have a reservation for this evening.
A2.why: Formal style: “do not” in full. English needs “do” to make “have” negative.

options: We are writing to thank you for your help.
We're writing to thank you for your help.
We writing to thank you for your help.
A2.why: “We are writing to…” is the classic formal opening, with the verb in full.

options: The company does not accept returns after 30 days.
The company doesn't accept returns after 30 days.
The company not accepts returns after 30 days.
B1.why: Company rules use “does not” in full; the negative needs “does” before “accept”.

options: We were unable to reach a decision.
We weren't able to reach a decision.
We was unable to reach a decision.
B1.why: “We were unable” is formal and complete; “we was” breaks the subject and verb agreement.

options: It would be appreciated if you could confirm.
It'd be appreciated if you could confirm.
It would be appreciate if you could confirm.
B1.why: “It would be appreciated” is a fixed formal phrase, in full and with the past participle.

options: I am not able to attend due to a prior commitment.
I'm not able to attend due to a prior commitment.
I amn't able to attend due to a prior commitment.
B1.why: “I am not” in full; “amn't” does not exist in standard English.

options: The board has not yet reviewed the proposal.
The board hasn't yet reviewed the proposal.
The board not has yet reviewed the proposal.
B1.why: “Has not” in full for formal writing; “not” goes after the auxiliary, never before it.

options: We do not anticipate any further delays.
We don't anticipate any further delays.
We not anticipate any further delays.
B1.why: Formal writing keeps “do not” in full; English needs “do” before “not” with most verbs.

options: She is not currently available for comment.
She isn't currently available for comment.
She not currently available for comment.
B1.why: Press statements use “is not” in full; the verb “is” cannot be left out.

options: You will not be charged for this service.
You won't be charged for this service.
You not be charged for this service.
B1.why: Customer letters write “will not” in full; the future needs “will”.

options: They cannot guarantee delivery by Friday.
They can't guarantee delivery by Friday.
They not can guarantee delivery by Friday.
B1.why: “Cannot” in full is the formal choice; “not can” is the Spanish order, not English.

options: The clinic will not be open during Fallas.
The clinic won't be open during Fallas.
The clinic will not to be open during Fallas.
B1.why: “Will not” in full for an official notice; after “will”, the verb takes no “to”.

options: The hotel does not allow pets in the rooms.
The hotel doesn't allow pets in the rooms.
The hotel not allows pets in the rooms.
B1.why: Formal rules use “does not” in full; “not allows” skips the auxiliary “does”.

options: The sheriff's office is not responsible for lost property.
The sheriff's office isn't responsible for lost property.
The sheriff's office not is responsible for lost property.
B1.why: Official notices write “is not” in full, and “not” always follows “is”.

options: The committee has not reached a consensus.
The committee hasn't reached a consensus.
The committee not has reached a consensus.
B2.why: Formal reports use “has not” in full; “not” follows the auxiliary, never the other way round.

options: It is not uncommon for delays to occur.
It's not uncommon for delays to occur.
It not uncommon for delays to occur.
B2.why: “It is not uncommon” is formal and stays in full; it means “it happens quite often”.

options: We would not recommend proceeding without approval.
We wouldn't recommend proceeding without approval.
We not recommend proceeding without approval.
B2.why: Professional advice uses “would not” in full; “we not recommend” misses the auxiliary.

options: The findings do not support this conclusion.
The findings don't support this conclusion.
The findings not support this conclusion.
B2.why: Academic writing avoids “don't”: “do not support”, in full.

options: I cannot stress enough the importance of this matter.
I can't stress enough the importance of this matter.
I not can stress enough the importance.
B2.why: “I cannot stress enough” is a formal set phrase, written in full.

options: The evidence is not sufficient to draw a conclusion.
The evidence isn't sufficient to draw a conclusion.
The evidence not sufficient to draw a conclusion.
B2.why: In academic writing, “is not sufficient” stays in full, with the verb “is”.

options: They will not be able to attend the ceremony.
They won't be able to attend the ceremony.
They not will be able to attend.
B2.why: Formal announcements write “will not” in full; “not” comes after “will”.

options: We have not received confirmation of your order.
We haven't received confirmation of your order.
We not received confirmation of your order.
B2.why: Business emails use “have not received” in full; the auxiliary “have” cannot be dropped.

options: This policy does not apply to existing customers.
This policy doesn't apply to existing customers.
This policy not apply to existing customers.
B2.why: Formal terms use “does not apply” in full; “not apply” misses “does”.

options: Early surgeons did not understand the importance of clean hands.
Early surgeons didn't understand the importance of clean hands.
Early surgeons not understood the importance of clean hands.
B2.why: Written history avoids contractions: “did not understand”, with “did” carrying the past.

options: The railway company has not yet compensated the passengers.
The railway company hasn't yet compensated the passengers.
The railway company not has yet compensated the passengers.
B2.why: Formal replies keep “has not” in full, with “not” after “has”.

options: We regret that the paella course is not available this month.
We regret that the paella course isn't available this month.
We regret that the paella course not is available this month.
B2.why: Formal notices write “is not available” in full; “not is” is the wrong order.

options: It would not be appropriate to comment further.
It wouldn't be appropriate to comment further.
It not be appropriate to comment further.
C1.why: Official statements write “would not” in full, especially in a polite refusal.

options: The report does not, in our view, reflect the facts.
The report doesn't, in our view, reflect the facts.
The report not, in our view, reflect the facts.
C1.why: With an aside like “in our view” in the middle, the full “does not” reads far more formally.

options: We cannot, under any circumstances, approve this request.
We can't, under any circumstances, approve this request.
We not can, under any circumstances, approve this request.
C1.why: “We cannot, under any circumstances” is a firm formal refusal; a contraction would soften it.

options: The panel was not, at that stage, in a position to decide.
The panel wasn't, at that stage, in a position to decide.
The panel not, at that stage, in a position to decide.
C1.why: Formal narrative keeps “was not” in full, even with a phrase inserted after “not”.

options: This matter has not previously been brought to our attention.
This matter hasn't previously been brought to our attention.
This matter not previously been brought.
C1.why: Official letters use “has not previously been” in full; every auxiliary must stay.

options: It is not, therefore, a straightforward decision.
It's not, therefore, a straightforward decision.
It not, therefore, a straightforward decision.
C1.why: “It is not, therefore,” in full; a contraction clashes with a formal linker like “therefore”.

options: We are not, at this juncture, able to comment.
We're not, at this juncture, able to comment.
We not, at this juncture, able to comment.
C1.why: “At this juncture” is very formal, so the verb stays in full: “We are not”.

options: The applicant did not meet the eligibility criteria.
The applicant didn't meet the eligibility criteria.
The applicant not meet the eligibility criteria.
C1.why: Official decisions use “did not meet” in full; the past needs “did” before “not”.

options: The board will not, under the circumstances, reconsider.
The board won't, under the circumstances, reconsider.
The board not, under the circumstances, reconsider.
C1.why: Formal decisions write “will not” in full, even when a phrase separates it from the verb.

options: Semmelweis's findings were not, at first, accepted by his colleagues.
Semmelweis's findings weren't, at first, accepted by his colleagues.
Semmelweis's findings not were, at first, accepted by his colleagues.
C1.why: Formal history writing: “were not” in full, with “not” after the verb “were”.

options: The town council could not, in good conscience, approve the plan.
The town council couldn't, in good conscience, approve the plan.
The town council not could, in good conscience, approve the plan.
C1.why: “Could not, in good conscience” is formal and full; “not could” is the Spanish order.

options: The territory had not, until then, been properly surveyed.
The territory hadn't, until then, been properly surveyed.
The territory not had, until then, been properly surveyed.
C1.why: Formal reports keep “had not” in full, with “not” after the auxiliary “had”.
